title: Systems Emergencies
summary: Oil, fuel, hydraulic, oxygen, trim, and landing gear emergency procedures.
overview: This event focuses on aircraft system malfunctions that can develop in flight. You will learn how to recognize and respond to oil, fuel, hydraulic, oxygen, trim, and landing gear emergencies while continuing to prioritize aircraft control, PEL setup, and when to land as soon as practical.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items
studyNotes.summary: Most of these malfunctions are handled by preserving what still works, minimizing extra power or configuration changes, and getting to the nearest suitable runway early.

items.text: A CHIP warning indicates possible metal contamination in the engine oil system.
Severe contamination can lead to engine failure with little warning.
Immediate actions:

children.text: PCL to minimum power required to intercept the ELP.

items.text: Higher power settings can make the problem worse.

sections.title: Oil System Malfunction / Low Oil Pressure

items.text: Symptoms may include:

children.text: Visible oil leaking from the aircraft.

items.text: A momentary amber OIL PX during maneuvering may not indicate a malfunction.
If both red and amber OIL PX messages appear with normal oil pressure, it may indicate an SCU failure.
If only the amber OIL PX caution appears:

children.text: Continue only if oil pressure is normal.

items.text: If the red OIL PX warning appears, amber OIL PX remains illuminated for more than 5 seconds, oil pressure fluctuates, or oil temperature is out of limits:

children.text: PCL to minimum power needed to intercept the ELP.

items.text: Low fuel pressure may be caused by:
Symptoms include:

children.text: BOOST PUMP advisory cycling on and off.

items.text: Immediate actions:
Do not reset the BOOST PUMP circuit breaker unless a greater emergency exists.
If the FUEL PX warning remains illuminated, the high pressure fuel pump is suction feeding and engine operation is time limited.
High fuel flow is considered 800 PPH or greater.
Immediate action:
High power settings combined with high ITT can make the condition worse.
Reducing power too aggressively can also risk engine flameout.
Symptoms include:
If normal hydraulic pressure is lost:

children.text: Landing gear, flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering should be considered unavailable.

items.text: If EHYD PX LO appears:

children.text: Emergency landing gear and flap extension system should be considered unavailable.

items.text: Gear and flaps should generally be lowered early if hydraulic fluid loss is suspected.
If all hydraulic fluid is lost, a gear-up landing may become necessary.
Low hydraulic pressure may require emergency landing gear extension.
Use this procedure only when directed by another malfunction checklist.
Pulling the Emergency Landing Gear Handle extends the gear regardless of gear handle position.
Once emergency extension is used:

children.text: Landing gear and flaps cannot be retracted.

items.text: Normal indications after emergency extension are:

children.text: Red light in the gear handle.

items.text: The pull may require significant force, sometimes over 80 pounds.
After landing, do not taxi if any gear position light indicates unsafe.
OBOGS FAIL indicates a malfunction in the oxygen system.
Causes may include:
Symptoms may include:
If any physiological symptoms occur:

children.text: Pull the Green Ring as required.

items.text: The emergency oxygen bottle lasts approximately 10 minutes.
Below 10,000 feet MSL:

children.text: Oxygen mask may be removed if required.

items.text: Land as soon as practical.
A runaway trim condition occurs when trim moves without pilot input.
The trim interrupt button or trim disconnect switch can be used to stop unwanted trim movement.
Pulling a trim circuit breaker makes that trim system inoperative.
Loss of rudder trim may significantly increase workload.
Maintain aircraft control first, then isolate the malfunction.
A PEL is used anytime a malfunction exists that may worsen before landing.
The goal is to safely reach the nearest suitable runway before the condition becomes an emergency.
Most system malfunctions in this event eventually lead to a PEL.
Focus on:

children.text: Preserving the aircraft systems that remain.

items.text: Aviate first.
Intercept the nearest suitable ELP early.
Avoid unnecessary power changes when a system malfunction is already developing.
Land as soon as practical before a manageable malfunction becomes a major emergency.
Many of these procedures are less about fixing the issue and more about preserving enough aircraft to safely land.
